title: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Chemical Plants (US)
description: Wet fluorescent MPI of carbon steel welds in US ammonia, caustic and fertilizer plants. Stainless and nickel alloys need penetrant. Request a quote.
h1: Magnetic Particle Inspection for Chemical Processing Plants in the United States
html:
Magnetic particle inspection (MPI) at a chemical plant has a narrow, valuable job: finding surface-breaking cracks in the carbon and low-alloy steel equipment that handles ammonia, caustic, fertilizer intermediates and industrial gases. Atlantis NDT mobilizes technicians to your plant anywhere in the United States to examine welds, nozzles, attachments, structural steel and rotating equipment with yokes and wet fluorescent particles. Austenitic stainless steel and nickel alloys are not magnetic, so we say plainly which equipment this method can and cannot cover. To scope a job, request a magnetic particle inspection quote.

Where MPI earns its place in chemical processing

Chemical plants have a lot of carbon steel, and a good deal of it sits in services that crack it. Anhydrous ammonia storage spheres and bullets are the classic case: ammonia stress corrosion cracking attacks welds in carbon steel, particularly where oxygen has entered the system or where the steel is hard, and wet fluorescent magnetic particle examination of the internal welds is the accepted way to look for it. Hot caustic lines and vessels in chlor-alkali, alumina and some specialty chemical plants can develop caustic cracking in carbon steel welds and heat-affected zones, and this mechanism is covered in industry guidance such as NACE SP0403 and API RP 571. Sour and wet hydrogen sulfide service, though more a refinery matter, appears in some chemical plants and produces similar surface-connected cracking at hard welds.

Beyond those mechanisms, ordinary fabrication and repair work needs MPI as well. New nozzle welds, pad-weld attachments, lifting lugs, vessel support welds, tank shell seams and weld repairs on pressure parts are routine candidates under ASME Section VIII and ASME B31.3 where the code or the owner's specification requires a surface examination after welding or post-weld heat treatment.

Codes, rules and who accepts the result

OSHA's Process Safety Management standard, 29 CFR 1910.119, requires covered plants to run a mechanical integrity program, and the EPA Risk Management Program in 40 CFR Part 68 adds hazard review requirements for facilities with listed substances. These rules do not prescribe how to run an MPI test. The pressure equipment codes do: ASME Section VIII for vessels, ASME B31.3 for process piping and the National Board Inspection Code for repairs. Many plants follow API 510 for vessels and API 570 for piping as part of their program, with alteration and repair examination requirements.

The method is written into the procedure from ASME Section V Article 7 and ASTM E1444, and the owner or fabricator's code says what examination coverage and which acceptance limits apply. Our explanation of Article 7 walks through the requirements. Acceptance is decided by the code table the contract names, applied by the plant's inspector or authorized inspector, and our report gives them the evidence. Atlantis technicians work under a written practice built on ASNT SNT-TC-1A; the Level II technician conducts the test and an ASNT Level III approves procedures and reviews reports before issue.

What equipment we examine

Ammonia and fertilizer storage. Spheres, bullets and refrigerated tanks. The technician examines the full length of selected welds from inside the vessel after cleaning, using wet fluorescent particles and a portable yoke, and records each crack-like indication with its location. Entry is controlled by the owner's confined space program.

Caustic and chlorine systems. Hot caustic lines, evaporators and heat exchangers in carbon steel are checked at welds, branch connections and bends. Where equipment has a stress-relieved weld requirement, the examination follows post-weld heat treatment so any cracking from the treatment shows.

Reactors, columns and process vessels. Nozzle-to-shell welds, reinforcement pad seams, skirt and support welds and internal attachments. After repair welding, the area is examined before hydrotest. We examine the weld and a band of adjacent base metal, as the procedure specifies.

Industrial gas equipment. Carbon steel tube trailers, cylinders, large receiver vessels and pipe racks. Oxygen service demands clean materials; we use particles and carriers approved by the owner for the service, and our procedure takes account of cleaning requirements before and after the test.

Structural steel and lifting hardware. Pipe rack welds, platform supports, crane hooks and lugs. See the pages on Houston magnetic particle testing for a regional example, and our overview of weld inspection for related coverage.

Rotating equipment. Shafts, impellers and fan hubs in carbon or alloy steel are examined for fatigue cracks at keyways, fillets and weld joins during a repair outage.

Equipment that magnetic particle cannot handle

Austenitic stainless steels such as 304 and 316, nickel alloys, aluminum and most titanium grades are not ferromagnetic and cannot be examined by MPI. That covers a great deal of corrosive-service chemical equipment. Duplex stainless steel has a partly magnetic structure and gives unreliable results, so penetrant testing is normally specified instead. In chloride-bearing environments, stress corrosion cracking of austenitic stainless is the main concern, and penetrant is the surface method, with the penetrant testing for chemical processing page covering it. Wall thickness loss from corrosion is not a surface-crack question at all; for that, see ultrasonic testing for chemical processing.

Low-alloy steel (chrome-moly)Works wellPenetrant on small areas
Austenitic stainlessCannot be usedPenetrant testing

The comparison of magnetic particle and penetrant testing gives the general trade-offs, and our national magnetic particle testing page covers the method outside chemical plants.

Technique for plant conditions

Wet fluorescent particles are the usual choice inside vessels, where darkness is easy to arrange and sensitivity matters. Visible particles suit outdoor structural work and larger fabrications. Before testing, the surface is cleaned to bare metal at the examination area: scale, paint, deposit and residue from the process can hide a crack or hold particles, so a wire brush, grinder or approved cleaner is used as the procedure allows. In ammonia and caustic service the surface may carry chemical residue that must be neutralized and removed.

The AC electromagnetic yoke is the workhorse because it is portable and the alternating field is concentrated near the surface. Yoke lifting power is verified before use. Each area is magnetized in two directions roughly at right angles so cracks of any orientation are caught. A pie gauge or a shim indicator proves the field is adequate for the geometry. Black-light intensity at the surface is measured with a calibrated meter, and ambient white light is kept low so indications are easy to read. Temperature limits matter: particle suspensions and some carriers are not suited to hot surfaces, so procedures state a working range and hot parts are cooled or examined with a technique qualified for the temperature.

After examination, parts are demagnetized where residual magnetism could affect welding, instrumentation or later service, and particle residue is cleaned from vessels so it does not become a contaminant in the process. We keep a note of the cleaning step in the report.

A typical vessel examination follows a set sequence so that nothing is missed. The technician reviews the weld map with the plant inspector and agrees which welds and what lengths are in scope. The surfaces are cleaned and a reference part or test ring is used to confirm that the particles, light and field are working before production examination starts. Each weld is scanned in two magnetizing directions, indications are flagged with a marker or a scribe, and photographs are taken before and after any grinding. If grinding is used to chase a crack, the examination is repeated on the ground area, and the final depth is recorded for the owner's engineer. Findings are discussed with the plant inspector at the end of each shift so repairs can be planned during the outage rather than after it.

What the report contains

  • Equipment tag, weld or component ID, material and location in the plant.
  • Procedure number, revision and the code and acceptance table applied.
  • Equipment and consumables: yoke or unit, lifting power, particle type and concentration, light meter reading.
  • Surface preparation, cleaning method and magnetization directions used.
  • Proof of field adequacy on the part or a representative section.
  • The examiner's qualification level under the written practice, and the ASNT Level III who approved the procedure.
  • Indication map with location, length and orientation, photographs and the accept or reject call.
  • Demagnetization and post-test cleaning.

What to send for a quote

  1. Equipment list with tag numbers, material, and weld or component types to be examined.
  2. The code, repair standard or program and its acceptance criteria, with weld maps or isometrics if available.
  3. Service and operating history, especially ammonia, caustic or hot service.
  4. Surface condition, coatings, insulation and linings.
  5. Access arrangements, confined space entry rules and darkness or lighting limits.
  6. Site address, badging, safe work permit rules and shutdown window.

Planning in a chemical plant

Examinations inside ammonia, chlorine or caustic equipment follow the owner's decontamination, gas testing and entry permit. We schedule alongside cleaning and scaffolding so technicians are not waiting for access, and we confirm lighting arrangements for fluorescent work before mobilizing. Where a plant requires intrinsically safe or non-sparking equipment in classified areas, we bring or request equipment approved for it; yokes and black lights are not interchangeable with hazardous-area rated units, and a part of the planning is a check on what area classification each task falls in.

We do not perform radiography in the United States and do not calculate remaining life or inspection intervals. Those belong to your engineer, your authorized inspector or a licensed contractor.

Where we work in the United States for chemical processing

  • Houston: Gulf Coast chemical complexes with repair and turnaround work year-round.
  • Baton Rouge: river corridor plants making commodity and specialty chemicals.
  • Lake Charles: chemical, gas and fertilizer-related plants near the Calcasieu Ship Channel.
  • Louisville: Ohio River chemical complexes with older carbon steel equipment.
  • Memphis: fertilizer and chemical storage along the Mississippi.
  • Newark: dense northern New Jersey chemical manufacturing.
  • Philadelphia: Delaware River chemical and industrial gas sites.
  • Buffalo: chlor-alkali and electrochemical heritage in western New York.

Training your own mag particle examiners

Plants that want their own examiners can enroll staff in SNT-TC-1A-based MT Level 1 training or MT Level 2 training and practice on the magnetic particle simulator. We can also draft your written practice or technical procedures so your own employer certification stands up in a PSM audit.

faq.q: Can magnetic particle inspection be used on stainless steel piping in a chemical plant?
faq.a: Not on austenitic grades such as 304 and 316, which are not ferromagnetic. Duplex stainless gives unreliable results as well. Penetrant testing is the surface method for those alloys, and we say so in the quote.

faq.q: Is MPI the right method to look for ammonia stress corrosion cracking?
faq.a: Wet fluorescent MPI of selected welds in carbon steel ammonia storage is the accepted surface method for this mechanism. It finds surface-connected cracks only, so your engineer decides how much weld length and which locations to examine.

faq.q: Do you test for caustic cracking in carbon steel welds?
faq.a: Yes, with wet fluorescent particles at welds, nozzles and bends in hot caustic service. The mechanism is described in industry guidance such as NACE SP0403 and API RP 571; the owner's engineer chooses locations and frequency.

faq.q: How does MPI fit into OSHA PSM mechanical integrity?
faq.a: 29 CFR 1910.119 requires inspection and testing of covered equipment by recognized good engineering practice. MPI is one tool the owner's program may call for, and our report gives the records, procedure and qualification data that audit files need.

faq.q: Who accepts or rejects the indications?
faq.a: The code table in your contract or repair standard decides, as applied by your inspector or authorized inspector. Atlantis records the indications and compares each to the named criteria; we do not decide fitness for service.

faq.q: Can you work in a classified hazardous area?
faq.a: We can, with equipment rated for the area classification, and the plan names which tasks fall in which classification. Tell us the classification at quote time so rated yokes and lights are brought.

faq.q: Is demagnetizing necessary after MPI on process equipment?
faq.a: Where residual magnetism could affect welding, instruments or later service, yes. The procedure states whether it is required, and the report records that it was done and the cleaning of particle residue from the vessel.

faq.q: Can you perform radiography on welds as an alternative?
faq.a: No. US industrial radiography falls under NRC and Agreement State licensing, which Atlantis does not hold, so we do not shoot films. Where your code permits, ultrasonic testing can supply the volumetric information.

faq.q: What do you need to quote MPI on chemical plant equipment?
faq.a: Equipment and weld list, materials, code and acceptance table, service history, surface condition and linings, access and entry rules, lighting limits and the site's badging and permit requirements.
